messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 67-year-old male, presented with severe shortness of breath and fast atrial fibrillation. Coronary angiogram revealed no significant coronary artery disease, CT scan revealed a large penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer at the junction of the distal ascending aorta and the undersurface of aortic arch, and echocardiogram showed grossly abnormal-looking distal ascending aorta with a large pseudoaneurysm in relation to the distal ascending aorta. The patient underwent aortic surgery and made an uncomplicated recovery.

The patient subsequently represented with worsening shortness of breath 6 months later and was found to have a large pseudoaneurysm in relation to the aortic arch. A redo sternotomy was performed, and the patient underwent total arch replacement. The false aneurysm cavity was extensively debrided and laid open. The patient had gradual respiratory weaning and required a percutaneous tracheostomy and antibiotics.

However, the patient's condition deteriorated suddenly after 6 weeks when a rupture and contrast leak of the descending thoracic aorta were discovered, along with a large hematoma. The patient underwent TEVAR with an excellent result. The patient also developed a pathological fracture of left proximal tibia and was diagnosed with metastatic renal cancer. The patient was referred to the palliative care team.

The patient continued to deteriorate and passed away peacefully 65 days following his total arch replacement.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Procedures:
Total arch replacement, TEVAR.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient passed away.

Instructions at Discharge:
None.

Follow-Up Care:
None.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The admission was driven by a large pseudoaneurysm of the aortic arch, a recurrence of the penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer and pseudoaneurysm, treated with total arch replacement. A later rupture of the descending thoracic aorta was treated with TEVAR. This is aortic aneurysm disease, chapter I, category I71; T81 could apply if the pseudoaneurysm were coded as a complication of the earlier surgery, but I71 is the better fit.
CODE: I71
